chapter: California, New York and Richard Himber
title: Himber's rhythmic pyramids and band-leader masks
summary: Himber's band changed styles, used masks to imitate leaders' themes on radio, causing mixups at the network.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: No, I was there for quite a few. We were there on, we started with Victor Records and then we went on another album, another company. We did a lot of, we did Studebaker transcriptions, a lot of stuff with Studebaker transcriptions. Well I think I was on drums most of those. You see he changed the style of the band every once in a while. He started off with this sort of bell tone band. You know, Bing-Bong, you know what the trumpet players, it's this band that if you played together you were wrong. Played pyramids a lot? Rhythmic Pyramids he used to call it. Rhythmic Pyramids, and the funny thing about it, we used to do them for our stage shows, he used to do the theme songs of different bands, and at the same time he would conduct the band, but he had a mask which were absolutely replicas of the leaders. I've never heard of that. Weidman, yeah, Weidman. We had, uh, Count Basie, uh, Artie Shaw, Benny Goodman. They were absolute replicas of these guys and he put on these things and he'd conduct them. How did you like the band doing that? Did they sound good? Oh, you couldn't tell the difference. In fact, there's a story I want to tell you about the thing that was, on two occasions, two occasions, two occasions we, there was a, we heard these stories in, in New York. This guy was listening to, we were coming on the air with, with Goodman's theme, and he was in a different room than the radio that was, and his wife was in the other, in the room with the radio, and all of a sudden, we stopped after about eight bars of the Goodman theme, we went into the Artie Shaw theme. And the guy said, quit fooling with the radio. He says, I wanted to hear Benny Goodman's program. She said, I haven't touched the radio. She said, oh yeah, okay then, leave it alone. So, after about sixteen bars of that, we come on with Count Basie's One O'Clock Jump. He says, quit playing with the radio, leave it alone. He says, I wanted to hear that then Artie Shaw. And the same thing happened, the same thing happened when we were working at the, at the nightclub in New York. What the hell is the name of that place? We were working there, and we used to do an NBC network show. And they never did, we never did have to clear the, we never did have to clear the introduction or the theme. So, he starts one night, and he's got, he's playing either Benny Goodman or Artie Shaw's theme. And we keep on playing it. And before you know it, they cut us off, and they, the telephone's ringing, and blah, blah, blah. The network, the control room over there, they think we all screwed up. They think that they're broadcasting from Shaw. They don't know that they got him, and they don't know what the hell's going on. Everything is all screwed up. So, from that time on, they made us tell us what the hell we were going to play, so that they wouldn't be messed up. But he was, the, uh, the, uh, the guy was, this, this, I got this to show you.
